claims.text: Adding a controlled amount of carbon to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve its glass-forming ability.
Adding carbon to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy will improve the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
The initial phosphorus-containing alloy may have a mixture or balance of crystalline and amorphous regions.
Carbon should be incorporated during alloy synthesis as a defined, controlled dopant addition.
The predicted comparison requires identical rapid-cooling and processing conditions for carbon-doped and undoped samples.
The beneficial effect requires carbon to be uniformly distributed.
The beneficial effect requires the carbon concentration to remain within its solubility limit.
Carbon dopants enhance atomic-scale structural disorder.
Carbon interferes with normal crystalline atomic packing and thereby impedes the growth of ordered phases.
Impeded nucleation and growth leave a higher fraction of the alloy in the amorphous state.
Carbon doping will produce a higher amorphous fraction than an otherwise comparable undoped phosphorus-containing alloy.
Carbon doping will raise the crystallization-onset temperature relative to an otherwise comparable undoped alloy.
Excessive carbon may cause phase separation or formation of unwanted compounds or phases that negate the benefits.
Processing conditions, including cooling conditions, may affect the extent of amorphization and phase transformation.
The optimum carbon concentration and magnitude of improvement are not yet specified.
XRD-derived amorphous fraction and DSC-derived crystallization-onset temperature can be used as experimental outcome variables.

Failure of carbon-doped samples to show a statistically significant increase in both amorphous fraction and crystallization-onset temperature, or observation of inferior properties, would falsify the hypothesis.
